Army|11B.title: Infantryman
Army|11B.intro: Infantry is far more than a path to police or security work. It builds decision-making under pressure, small-unit leadership, mission planning, communications, land navigation, weapons safety, and first aid. Those are transferable leadership and operations capabilities that open doors in trades, operations, public safety, training, and government, not a single career lane.
capabilities: Small-unit leadership and decision-making under stress
Tactical combat casualty care (first aid under pressure)
paths: Discipline, teamwork, and working safely in tough conditions transfer well to construction and industrial trades.
Enter a registered/union apprenticeship (e.g., Helmets to Hardhats); no trade license is implied by service.
Leading teams, enforcing standards, and hitting objectives maps to frontline operations leadership.
Translate team size, tempo, and outcomes into civilian terms; Lean fundamentals help.
Casualty care, composure, and teamwork support EMS and fire work.
Earn EMT or firefighter certification; state licensure is separate from military training.
One credible option among many, not the default; leadership and judgment apply.
Complete a police academy / POST; background and fitness standards apply.
Planning people, equipment, and timelines under constraints maps to project delivery.
OSHA 10/30 and CAPM can bridge terminology.
Risk awareness and disciplined execution support protective and security operations roles.
Clearance eligibility and state guard/PI licensing may be required.
Cadre and range-cadre experience supports workforce training and safety instruction.
Document audience size and outcomes; instructional-design basics help.
bands: Lead with individual and team tasks, weapons and equipment qualifications, first-aid training, physical standards, and the conditions you operated in. Do not inflate supervisory scope.
E-5–E-6 / NCO
Add team/squad leadership: soldiers led, training delivered, mission planning, standards enforcement, and accountability for people and sensitive equipment.
E-7–E-9 / Senior NCO
Emphasize platoon/company operations, planning and rehearsals, personnel development, resource and readiness management, and advising senior leaders.

Army|12B.title: Combat Engineer
Army|12B.intro: Combat engineering is much broader than law enforcement. It combines construction, route and terrain reconnaissance, heavy equipment, demolition safety, obstacle reduction, logistics, and small-team problem solving. Those capabilities can open several civilian and government directions; they do not limit a veteran to one field.
capabilities: Route, bridge, terrain, and obstacle reconnaissance
Light and heavy engineer vehicle operation
paths: Field coordination, site preparation, materials, safety, and work sequencing transfer directly.
OSHA 10/30; document project scope and equipment used.
Engineer vehicle operation transfers to earthmoving, utilities, roadwork, and site development.
State or employer equipment qualification; a CDL widens options.
Reconnaissance, route analysis, terrain reading, and reporting support technical field work.
Learn civilian GIS/CAD tools; licensure is not implied.
Risk assessment, contingency planning, and operating under pressure support disaster work.
FEMA Independent Study courses translate exercises into planning outcomes.
Hazard recognition, controls, and pre-operation checks are valuable safety experience.
OSHA credential; ASP/CSP require separate eligibility.
Planning people, equipment, timelines, and requirements maps to project delivery.
CAPM or construction scheduling fundamentals can bridge terminology.
Demolition planning and explosives safety may relate to regulated blasting, mining, or public safety.
Civilian licensing, background checks, and employer training are mandatory.
bands: Lead with hands-on construction/demolition tasks, engineer equipment operated, safety discipline, and field conditions. Do not inflate supervisory scope.
E-5–E-6 / NCO
Add squad leadership, training, work allocation, quality control, and the people or equipment you directly supervised.
E-7–E-9 / Senior NCO
Emphasize multi-team operations, project scheduling, resource forecasting, safety systems, and organization-level results.

Army|68W.title: Combat Medic Specialist
Army|68W.intro: A combat medic is not just an EMT. The role covers emergency and trauma care, patient assessment, medication administration under protocol, medical documentation, medical logistics, and clinic support, often while leading and training others. That range supports many clinical, logistics, public-health, and healthcare-administration directions, though civilian roles still require their own licensure.

Medical supply, equipment, and logistics accountability
Sick call and outpatient clinic support

PA school required (active-duty IPAP is one route).

A CRCST or supply credential strengthens the move.

A community-health-worker certificate helps in many states.

E-5–E-6 / NCO
Add section-medic leadership: junior medics trained, clinic/treatment-team supervision, protocols enforced, and readiness tracking.
E-7–E-9 / Senior NCO
Emphasize medical operations planning, personnel and equipment management, program oversight, and advising commanders on medical readiness.

Army|88M.title: Motor Transport Operator
Army|88M.intro: Motor transport is more than driving a truck. It covers convoy planning and execution, load planning and cargo securement, vehicle inspection and fault reporting, hazardous-materials handling, and movement tracking and accountability, often leading teams and managing fleets. That opens driving, logistics, fleet-management, safety, and government directions.

HazMat endorsement and 49 CFR training are required.

Equipment-specific qualification; a CDL widens options.

E-5–E-6 / NCO
Add convoy or dispatch leadership: drivers led, movement planning, safety and licensing oversight, and the assets you managed.
E-7–E-9 / Senior NCO
Emphasize movement control, multi-team operations, maintenance and safety programs, and resource/readiness forecasting.

Army|91B.title: Wheeled Vehicle Mechanic
Army|91B.intro: A wheeled vehicle mechanic does far more than 'turn wrenches.' The work covers engine and powertrain diagnostics, electrical and hydraulic troubleshooting, preventive maintenance, use of technical manuals and test equipment, and field repair under constraints, often leading a shop. That supports automotive/diesel, fleet, field-service, quality, and maintenance-management directions.

Technical manuals, schematics, and test equipment
Field and battle-damage repair under constraints
Parts, tools, and maintenance records management

OEM/product training; translate platforms into systems and fault-isolation methods.

OEM certification for specific equipment lines helps.

CMMS experience and planning credentials help.

Add shop/section leadership: mechanics led, quality control, training, and the equipment value and readiness you managed.
E-7–E-9 / Senior NCO
Emphasize maintenance operations, shop management, readiness and resource forecasting, and safety/quality programs.

Army|92Y.title: Unit Supply Specialist
Army|92Y.intro: A unit supply specialist is not just a stock clerk. The role covers property accountability, inventory control, requisition and receipt processing, supply-system data entry, records and audits, and management of hazardous and sensitive items, often supervising a supply room. That supports inventory, procurement, logistics-analysis, warehouse-management, and government property directions.

E-7–E-9 / Senior NCO
Emphasize supply operations, multi-unit accountability, financial and resource oversight, and process improvement results.

Army|11C.intro: Indirect fire (mortars) is not just an infantry-to-security path. Army|13B.title: Cannon Crewmember

Army|35F.intro: Intelligence analysts research, evaluate, and synthesize information, brief decision-makers, and work with analytic tools and databases, often holding a security clearance.
